title: Use Every Ticket Once
statement:
You find a stack of plane tickets. Each tickets[i] = [from, to] is one flight between two airports, written as three-letter codes. You start at airport start and must use every ticket exactly once, each flight leaving from the airport where the previous one landed.

Return the airports in the order you visit them (that is tickets.length + 1 codes, beginning with start). At least one such route is guaranteed to exist. If several routes work, return the one that comes first in alphabetical order, comparing the routes airport by airport.

The same ticket can appear more than once; each copy is a separate flight that must be used.

examples.why: Flying to BER first looks right alphabetically, but BER has no ticket out, so the ROM tickets would be left unused. The only full route visits ROM first.
Both loops can go first and both orders use every ticket. HND comes before ICN, so that loop goes first.
The two AMS → LIS tickets are separate flights, and both must be used.

constraints: Every code is three uppercase English letters
At least one route that uses every ticket exists
hints: Airports are nodes and tickets are edges. You need a walk that uses every edge exactly once. Trying the alphabetically smallest flight each time fails when it leads into a dead end too early, as in example 1.
Backtracking works but can be exponential. Think about the dead end differently: the airport you get stuck at must be the last stop of the whole route.

Hierholzer's algorithm: walk greedily, always taking the smallest unused ticket. When an airport has no tickets left, it goes onto the front of the answer and you step back. Build the route in reverse as airports get stuck, then reverse it.

explain.intuition:
Treat airports as nodes and tickets as directed edges. A route that uses every edge once is an Eulerian path. Greedy "take the smallest ticket" goes wrong only one way: it walks into an airport where you get stuck while tickets remain elsewhere. But getting stuck tells you something. When you are stuck at an airport with no tickets out, that airport must be the end of the route, because nothing can follow it.

Hierholzer's algorithm turns this into a rule. Walk greedily with a stack, always taking the alphabetically smallest unused ticket from the airport on top. When the top airport has no tickets left, pop it and add it to the result. Popped airports come out in reverse route order. The detours you skipped (like the ROM loop in example 1) get walked when you step back to them, and they are spliced in before the part already finished. Reversing the result gives the route. Because every choice took the smallest ticket available, and a later choice is only ever pushed further back when it really was a dead end, the result is the alphabetically first route.
steps: Group tickets by departure airport and sort each group so the smallest destination is taken first (in code: sort descending and pop from the end).
While the stack is not empty: if the top airport still has tickets, remove its smallest one and push the destination.
Otherwise pop the top airport and append it to route.
pitfalls: Plain greedy without backtracking or Hierholzer: example 1 gets stuck at BER with tickets left.
Treating duplicate tickets as one. Each copy must be used, so keep a list per airport, not a set.
Writing the stack walk recursively. A 20 000-ticket route recurses 20 000 deep, past Python's default limit. The explicit stack avoids it.

complexity.time: O(E log E) for sorting the tickets; the walk itself is O(E)

solutions.title: Backtracking in alphabetical order
solutions.idea: Try tickets from the current airport in sorted order. If the route gets stuck before using every ticket, undo the last ticket and try the next. The first complete route found is the alphabetically first.

solutions.title: Hierholzer's algorithm
solutions.idea: Walk greedily with a stack, always taking the smallest unused ticket. An airport with nothing left is final: pop it into the answer. Reverse at the end.

followups: No route is guaranteed. How do you check, before walking, whether one exists? (Compare each airport's tickets in and out.)
The tickets are undirected: a ticket between A and B can be flown either way. What changes?
